key.title: Laying Plans
key.main_idea: Sun Tzu says war is a matter of life and death, so it must be studied carefully before anything is done. Success comes from honest comparison on five basic factors and from careful calculation in advance; the side that plans more usually wins.

key_lessons.text: Serious matters deserve serious study. Sun Tzu calls war "a road either to safety or to ruin".
key_lessons.source_snippet: It is a matter of life and death, a road either to safety or to ruin.

key_lessons.text: Judge any situation by five factors: the Moral Law (unity with your people), Heaven (timing and seasons), Earth (terrain and distance), the Commander (the leader's qualities) and Method and discipline (organisation and money).
key_lessons.source_snippet: The Moral Law; (2) Heaven; (3) Earth; (4) The Commander; (5) Method and discipline.

key_lessons.text: Compare honestly with your opponent: who has the better leader, the stronger team, the stricter discipline, the fairer rewards?
key_lessons.source_snippet: By means of these seven considerations I can forecast victory or defeat.

key_lessons.text: Plans must bend to circumstances. Rules are a guide, not a cage.
key_lessons.source_snippet: According as circumstances are favorable, one should modify one's plans.

key_lessons.text: Calculation before action decides the result: many calculations lead to victory, few to defeat.
key_lessons.source_snippet: Thus do many calculations lead to victory, and few calculations to defeat

key.takeaway: Before any big move, sit down and compare your position honestly on a few key factors. The side that prepares more thoroughly usually wins.

quick_check.question: What does Sun Tzu say decides who will win, before the battle even starts?
options: How many careful calculations each side makes beforehand
Which side is braver on the day
Which side has more soldiers, nothing else
quick_check.simpler_explanation: Sun Tzu says the winner is usually decided in planning. The general who thinks through many details before acting wins; the one who plans little loses.

reflection_questions: Which important decision in your work or life right now deserves more "calculation in the temple" before you act?
If you compared yourself honestly with a competitor on leadership, team, discipline and rewards, where would you be weaker?
Where are you holding on to a plan even though circumstances have changed?
key.coverage_note: This edition (Lionel Giles) mixes Sun Tzu's text with commentators' notes in brackets; examples marked From the book may come from those notes.

examples.text: In this edition the translator adds a story about Wellington before Waterloo: asked for his plans, he replied that they depended on what Bonaparte did first. It shows why plans must adapt.
examples.source_snippet: Who will attack the first tomorrow -- I or Bonaparte?

examples.text: A commentator's note tells of a general so strict about his own rule against damaging crops that, when his horse strayed into a field, he punished himself by cutting off his hair.
examples.source_snippet: he condemned himself to death for having allowed his horse to shy into a field of corn

examples.text: A small shop planning to open a second branch can use the five factors: team unity, the right season, the location, the manager's ability, and systems and cash.

examples.takeaway: Before any big move, sit down and compare your position honestly on a few key factors. The side that prepares more thoroughly usually wins.

complete.title: Laying Plans
complete.main_idea: Sun Tzu says war is a matter of life and death, so it must be studied carefully before anything is done. Success comes from honest comparison on five basic factors and from careful calculation in advance; the side that plans more usually wins.

sections.heading: Why careful study matters
sections.explanation: Sun Tzu begins by saying that war is of vital importance: a matter of life and death, a road to safety or to ruin. For that reason it can never be approached carelessly. The same seriousness applies to any decision with big consequences.

examples.text: His opening lines set the tone.
examples.source_snippet: It is a matter of life and death, a road either to safety or to ruin.

sections.heading: The five constant factors
sections.explanation: Every situation should be judged on five factors. The Moral Law means people are united with their leader. Heaven means timing: night and day, heat and cold, seasons. Earth means distances, danger and terrain. The Commander stands for wisdom, sincerity, benevolence, courage and strictness. Method and discipline means organisation, ranks, supply routes and control of spending.

examples.text: Sun Tzu lists the five qualities of a commander.
examples.source_snippet: The COMMANDER stands for the virtues of wisdom, sincerity, benevolence, courage and strictness.

sections.heading: Seven questions to compare both sides
sections.explanation: Turn the five factors into questions: whose ruler is in harmony with the people, whose general is more able, who has the advantages of timing and terrain, where discipline is stricter, whose army is stronger, whose people are better trained, and who rewards and punishes more consistently. With these, Sun Tzu says, he can forecast victory or defeat.

examples.text: A note tells of a general who punished himself when his own horse damaged crops, to show that rules apply to leaders too.
examples.source_snippet: he condemned himself to death for having allowed his horse to shy into a field of corn

sections.heading: Adapt the plan
sections.explanation: Good counsel should be combined with whatever helpful circumstances appear. Plans must change as conditions change; rigid rules lose to a flexible opponent.

examples.text: The translator's story of Wellington refusing to fix his plans before knowing Bonaparte's.
examples.source_snippet: Who will attack the first tomorrow -- I or Bonaparte?

sections.heading: Deception and timing
sections.explanation: Sun Tzu says all warfare is based on deception: appear weak when strong, far when near, and attack where the other side is unprepared. In everyday work the useful lesson is less about tricking people and more about not revealing every plan too early and choosing your moment well.

sections.heading: Many calculations win
sections.explanation: The general who wins makes many calculations before the battle; the one who loses makes few, and with no calculation at all there is no hope. Preparation, Sun Tzu concludes, lets you foresee who is likely to win.

examples.text: The chapter closes on this point.
examples.source_snippet: Thus do many calculations lead to victory, and few calculations to defeat
